content.canonical: Both global unstructured magnitude pruning, which applies a uniform sparsity ratio across all weights, and fine-grained layer-wise magnitude pruning, which applies per-layer magnitude thresholds, substantially reduce on-disk model size when the model state is stored sparsely by keeping only nonzero weight values and their positions.
Fine-grained layer-wise pruning, when applied without fine-tuning, yields larger accuracy drops than global unstructured pruning.
(on Cora node classification, accuracy drops from 0.86 at baseline to 0.76 at 90% sparsity without fine-tuning),
When followed by fine-tuning, fine-grained layer-wise pruning can recover or surpass baseline accuracy on structurally sensitive tasks.
(accuracy recovers to approximately 0.89 at 90% sparsity after fine-tuning).
On tasks other than structurally sensitive tasks, fine-grained pruning with fine-tuning does not recover baseline accuracy at high sparsity.
Global pruning is lower-variance than fine-grained pruning.
Global pruning is safer for general compression than fine-grained pruning.
Fine-grained pruning is higher-variance than global pruning.
Fine-grained pruning may preserve critical substructures.
Fine-grained pruning may yield better accuracy recovery than global pruning on some datasets.
Empirically, pruned models achieve size reductions of approximately 4–9× at high sparsity (80–90%), depending on dataset and method.

Layer-wise analysis of sparsity under global unstructured magnitude pruning applied to the GNN architectures (GNNNet on BBBP, SplineConv on Cora node classification, HGP-SL on Proteins) reveals heterogeneous sensitivity to pruning.
Early convolutional layers maintain a low proportion of zero weights even at high global sparsity targets.
Early convolutional layers exhibit tolerance to pruning even at high global sparsity targets.
Linear projection layers and final classifier MLPs exhibit a high proportion of zero weights even at low global sparsity.
Linear projection layers and final classifier MLPs exhibit greater sensitivity to pruning than early convolutional layers.
In the experiments on GNN architectures and datasets, reductions in parameter count from pruning did not translate into consistent decreases in inference time or memory usage.
Inference latency remained largely unchanged across sparsity levels.
Memory usage and CPU/energy consumption showed non-monotonic, dataset- and sparsity-dependent patterns.
For global pruning, CPU usage peaks at 70% sparsity across datasets.
For fine-grained pruning, CPU and energy consumption exhibit sharp spikes and bimodal profiles.
global pruning on the Cora node classification task achieves a baseline-to-pruned size ratio of 4.76× at 80% sparsity and 8.98× at 90% sparsity.
For fine-grained pruning, energy consumption is higher than for global pruning at low-to-moderate sparsities.
Global pruning is more energy-efficient than fine-grained pruning at medium-to-high sparsities.

Empirically, significant reductions in on-disk model sizes appear when sparsity exceeds roughly 80%.
Storing sparse indices and metadata offsets incurs overhead at lower sparsities.

Evaluating quantization schemes on the GIN graph-classification model reveals that Degree-Quant with INT8 and Quantization-Aware Training with INT8 consistently recover most or all accuracy lost to reduced precision and often improve resource metrics.
For the BBBP dataset, DQ-INT8 achieves accuracy 0.83 ± 0.01, inference time 2.04 s, and energy 24.78 ± 0.17 J;

On the GIN graph-classification model, for the BBBP dataset, Quantization-Aware Training with INT8 (QAT-INT8) achieves accuracy and inference time similar to Degree-Quant with INT8, but higher energy than Degree-Quant with INT8.
For the Proteins dataset, DQ-INT8 achieves accuracy 0.72 ± 0.01 and energy 28.74 ± 2.72 J;

In the evaluated pruning experiments, fine-grained pruning showed high risk and high reward, performing well on particular tasks only with fine-tuning and causing excessively aggressive degradation without it.
Global pruning was more reliable across tasks than fine-grained pruning, with particular strength in link prediction.

On the BBBP and Cora-Node datasets, the combination of fine-grained pruning and fine-tuning proved more effective than fine-grained pruning alone, mitigating the substantial decreases in accuracy caused by pruning.
